```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, message = FALSE)
has_data <- requireNamespace("StMoMo", quietly = TRUE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE) && has_data
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_data)
```

Two questions are easily confused:

* **Tuning**: which settings of a model forecast best? For example the
  number of years the model is fitted to, the number of components, or
  the smoothing parameter. Tuning tries several settings and keeps the
  one that forecast the last observed years best.
* **Recalibration**: how wide should the intervals be? A model's intervals
  describe the uncertainty of its own assumptions. Recalibration rescales
  them so that they match the errors the model made in recent years.

Tuning changes the forecast itself; recalibration keeps the model and its
central forecast and changes the width of the intervals. Both use only
the training data, so they can be checked in a backtest (see
"Backtesting and scores"). The examples use Lee-Carter on England & Wales
men, ages 30-100, 1961-2011 (Human Mortality Database, via the StMoMo
package).

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
ew <- as_mt_data(StMoMo::EWMaleData)
ew <- mt_regroup(mt_set_grid(ew, age = single_ages(30, 100, open = FALSE)), age = single_ages(30, 100, open = FALSE))
```

## Tuning: the fitting window

Mortality decline in England & Wales changed pace in the 1970s. Lee-Carter
fitted to all years since 1961 averages over both regimes. A shorter
fitting window follows the recent pace but rests on fewer years. Which
window forecasts best? `mt_tune()` fits each candidate to the years up to
2001, forecasts 2002-2011 (a hold-out of the last ten years) and scores
the forecasts. The window is a preprocessing step (`step_window()`), so
the candidate is a model with its preprocessing:

```{r}
window_model <- function(window) list(spec = lee_carter(), prep = mt_prep(step_window(window)))
tn <- mt_tune(window_model, data.frame(window = c(15, 20, 30, 51)), ew, inner_origins = 1, inner_h = 10,
              metric = "rmse")
tn$scores
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 2.5}
mt_plot_tuning(tn)
```

`rmse` is the root mean squared error of the forecast median of the log
rates; the bars show one standard error. The last 15 years forecast the
held-out decade best, but the neighbouring window of 20 years lies only
about one standard error behind: with a single hold-out, such a choice is
uncertain. `tuned()` wraps this choice into a model: whenever
it is fitted, it repeats the tuning on the data it receives and then fits
the chosen setting to all of them.

`inner_origins = 1` is a single hold-out. Several origins
(`inner_origins = 3, inner_h = 5`) average over more periods, and
`select = "one_se"` keeps the simplest setting whose score is within one
standard error of the best. `target = "life_expectancy"` tunes for life
expectancy instead of the rates.

Tuning pays where a setting changes the forecast substantively and
consistently. In outer backtests on England & Wales and France
(`dev/tuning.md` in the source repository) the tuned window improved
Lee-Carter clearly, while tuning the number of components and the
smoothing of `hyndman_ullah()` the same way did not: the chosen setting
changed from one year to the next, a sign that the differences between
the settings were mostly noise of the held-out years.

## Recalibration: the width of the intervals

`recalibrated()` refits the model at several origins within the last ten
training years, compares the forecasts with what was observed, and
rescales the spread of the draws around their median by a factor that
can grow with the horizon. The factor minimises the CRPS of these recent
forecasts:

```{r}
fit_cal <- mt_fit(recalibrated(lee_carter()), ew)
fit_cal$calibration[, .(scale_h1, slope, crps_before, crps_after, cov95_before, cov95_after)]
```

The factor at horizon 1 (`scale_h1`) is about 2.7: Lee-Carter's
intervals were far too narrow in the last decade. The factor changes
little with the horizon (`slope` near 0, the factor is `scale_h1 * h^slope`).
Within the window, recalibration raised the 95% coverage from 0.67 to 0.93.

## Both together, checked in a backtest

The four versions in a backtest from the origins 1996-2001, forecasting
ten years each; tuning and recalibration are repeated at every origin from
its own training data:

```{r}
tuned_lc <- tuned(window_model, data.frame(window = c(15, 20, 30, 51)), inner_origins = 1, inner_h = 10,
                  metric = "rmse", label = "Lee-Carter, window tuned")
bt <- mt_compare(list("Lee-Carter" = lee_carter(), "window tuned" = tuned_lc,
                      "recalibrated" = recalibrated(lee_carter()), "window tuned, recalibrated" = recalibrated(tuned_lc)),
                 ew, origins = 1996:2001, h = 10, n_draws = 200, quantities = "life_expectancy")
mt_score_table(bt, metrics = c("crps", "cov95"))
```

```{r, eval = has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
mt_plot_coverage(bt)
```

The tuned window makes the forecasts more accurate: CRPS 0.057 against
0.069 for the rates, 0.29 against 0.47 years for life expectancy at 30
(`_le`). Recalibration widens the intervals: the 95% coverage of the rates
rises from 0.75 to 0.88, and from 0.73 to 0.83 for the tuned model,
whose recent errors were smaller, so its intervals widen less. The
coverage of life expectancy is high for all versions: errors of single
ages partly cancel in life expectancy. Tuning and recalibration answer
different questions and combine: the tuned and recalibrated version has the
lowest CRPS of the rates (0.056).

## Options

* `recalibrated(by = "sex")`: separate factors for groups of strata (with
  joint models, contrasts between the groups then get wider intervals);
* `recalibrated(ages = c(50, 75))`: separate factors for age bands;
* `recalibrated(quantity = "life_expectancy")`: recalibrate the intervals of
  life expectancy instead of single rates;
* `recalibrated(n_boot = 50)`: bootstrap intervals of the factors, which
  rest on few forecasts;
* `tuned(..., by = "sex")`: tune and fit groups of strata separately.

## Summary

| Question | Function | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| Which settings forecast best? | `mt_tune()`, `tuned()` | the forecast |
| How wide should the intervals be? | `recalibrated()` | the width of the intervals |
| Did it help? | `mt_compare()`, `mt_score_table()` | nothing; it checks |
